The transformation of ordinary sand into the transparent, versatile material we know as glass is a fascinating industrial process that combines ancient alchemy with modern engineering. While the basic recipe has remained largely unchanged for millennia, the scale and precision of modern manufacturing have evolved significantly. The journey begins with the raw materials, primarily silica sand, which constitutes about 70% of the final product. This sand is not just any beach sand; it must be highly purified to remove impurities like iron, which would otherwise give the glass an unwanted green tint. To this silica, manufacturers add soda ash (sodium carbonate) and limestone (calcium carbonate). Soda ash acts as a flux, lowering the melting point of the silica from an impractical 2,000°C to a more manageable 1,700°C, while limestone serves as a stabilizer, preventing the glass from dissolving in water.

These raw ingredients are carefully measured and mixed in a process called batching. The mixture is then fed into a massive furnace, often a regenerative tank furnace, where it is subjected to intense heat.
